lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: Ember, a Language of Our Own
text: Welcome to Build a Programming Language. Over this course we are going to design a small programming language of our own, and then build everything that is needed to run it, from scratch, in plain JavaScript. No parser generators, no libraries, no magic. I'm going to call the language Ember, because it's small, it's warm, and it's the kind of thing that can set a lot on fire if you let it. By the end, you will be able to write an Ember program in a text file, hand it to a tool you built, and watch it run. And more importantly, you will know exactly why it runs, because you wrote every line of the machinery.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: Ember, a Language of Our Own
text: Let me show you what Ember looks like, so the goal is concrete. We declare variables with the keyword `let`, like `let x = 5;`. We declare functions with the keyword `fn`, like `fn add(a, b) { return a + b; }`. We have `if` and `else`, we have `while` loops, and functions are values, which means you can return one function from another and it remembers the variables around it. That's a closure, and yes, we will build those. Statements end with a semicolon, strings use double quotes, and a line comment starts with two slashes. That's nearly the whole language, and it's deliberately small so that nothing hides from us.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: Ember, a Language of Our Own
text: Now, what do we actually build? Three programs, really, plus a little glue. First is the tokenizer, in a file called tokenizer.js. It takes the raw text of an Ember program and chops it into tokens, which are the words and punctuation of the language. Second is the parser, in parser.js. It takes that flat list of tokens and builds a tree, called an abstract syntax tree, that captures the structure of the program. Third is the interpreter, in interpreter.js, which walks that tree and does what it says. Source text goes in one end, behavior comes out the other end. Each stage has one job, and each stage only talks to the next.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: Ember, a Language of Our Own
text: You might wonder why we are building an interpreter and not a compiler. Two reasons. First, a tree-walking interpreter is the shortest path from nothing to a working language. You can have something running in an afternoon. Second, the front half, the tokenizer and parser, is exactly the same in a compiler. So you are not learning a toy idea, you are learning the half that every real language shares. Later in the course we will look at how compilers, interpreters, transpilers and the JIT inside V8 differ, so you can see where our design sits among them, and why real engines do more work than we will.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: Ember, a Language of Our Own
text: Here is how the course is laid out. We start with first principles. We'll look at how languages evolved from machine code to JavaScript, and we'll borrow ideas from human grammar to understand what syntax and semantics really mean. Then we break a language into its parts: values, datatypes, expressions, variables, scope and control flow. After that we look at how source code travels down to bytecode and machine code. Only then do we start building. We write Ember's grammar in BNF, then the tokenizer, then the parser, then the interpreter, and finally we run a real, slightly interesting program end to end.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: Ember, a Language of Our Own
text: A quick word on what you need. You need to be comfortable with JavaScript: functions, objects, arrays, classes, and the idea of recursion. If recursion makes you nervous, that's fine, we will go slowly, because the parser is basically recursion wearing a tie. You need Node installed, any recent version, and an editor. Make a folder called ember, and inside it we will end up with tokenizer.js, parser.js, interpreter.js and a small runner. Nothing else. No npm install. That's a promise, and I like keeping it.

lecture_title: 1.1 - What We Will Build: Ember, a Language of Our Own
text: One thing I want you to take from this course beyond Ember itself. Languages feel like fixed, sacred things handed down by committees. They are not. A language is a grammar, a handful of rules about meaning, and a program that enforces both. Once you have built one, every language you use afterwards becomes more transparent. You see why a missing bracket gives that particular error, why a variable is visible here but not there, and why one language is fast and another is slow. Okay? In the next lecture we begin at the beginning, with machine code, and we walk the history all the way to JavaScript.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Language History: From Machine Code to JavaScript
text: Before we write any Ember, I want to give you a little history, because every design decision we make later has an ancestor. Let's start at the bottom. A computer's processor understands exactly one thing, and that is machine code: numbers. A particular pattern of bits means add these two registers, another means jump to this address. Early programmers literally wrote those numbers by hand, sometimes flipping switches. It works, but it is brutal. You cannot read it a week later, you cannot move it to a different processor, and a single wrong digit gives you a crash with no explanation at all.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Language History: From Machine Code to JavaScript
text: The first improvement was assembly language. Instead of writing the number for add, you write the word `ADD`. Instead of a raw address, you write a label. A small program called an assembler translates these names back into numbers, one for one. That was a big deal, because it introduced the idea that a program is text that gets translated, rather than numbers we type directly. But assembly is still tied to one machine. Each instruction maps to one processor instruction, so code for one family of chips is useless on another. You are still thinking like the hardware, not like a person solving a problem.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Language History: From Machine Code to JavaScript
text: So came high-level languages. Fortran in the fifties let you write formulas that looked like mathematics, and a compiler turned them into machine code. Lisp showed up around the same time with an idea that is very relevant for us: code could be represented as a tree, and a program could evaluate that tree. COBOL aimed at business users. Then in the seventies, C gave us a language close enough to the machine to write operating systems, yet portable enough to compile on many chips. Notice the trend. Each step moves further from the hardware and closer to how humans think, and each step needs a smarter translator.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Language History: From Machine Code to JavaScript
text: In the eighties and nineties the big idea was objects and portability. C++ added classes to C. Java said write once, run anywhere, by compiling to a bytecode that runs on a virtual machine, which is a program pretending to be a computer. Python and Ruby leaned on interpreters, so you could run code the moment you wrote it, trading speed for convenience. Notice that nobody is replacing the previous layer. Everything is stacked. A Python program is run by an interpreter written in C, which is compiled to machine code, which is executed by the processor. Languages are built out of other languages, all the way down.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Language History: From Machine Code to JavaScript
text: And then JavaScript. In 1995, Brendan Eich built the first version of it in about ten days at Netscape, to make web pages interactive. It was meant to be small and forgiving, and it was originally interpreted inside the browser. As web apps grew, interpreting became too slow, so engines like V8 in Chrome started compiling JavaScript to machine code while it runs, which is called just-in-time compilation. We will unpack that later in the course. For now, notice the story: a language designed in ten days ended up on every phone and server, because someone wrote a good interpreter for it.

lecture_title: 1.2 - Language History: From Machine Code to JavaScript
text: Here is the takeaway for us. Ember sits on that very same timeline, at the interpreter end. Our tree-walking design is roughly what early JavaScript engines and early Lisp systems did. It is not fast, but it is clear, and it teaches every idea the fast engines also depend on. We will write Ember in JavaScript, so there is a nice loop here: a language, running on a language, running on machine code. The question we will keep asking is what a language really is. In the next chapter we borrow some answers from an unexpected place: the grammar of human languages like English.

lecture_title: 2.1 - What Human Languages Teach Us About Grammar
text: Let's start this lecture with a sentence: the dog chased the cat. You understood it instantly. Now another: chased cat the dog the. Same words, and it is gibberish. Nothing about the individual words changed, only the arrangement. That is the first thing human languages teach us. A language is not a bag of words, it is words plus rules about how they can be arranged. Those rules are what linguists call grammar, and a programming language needs the same thing, just with much stricter rules, because the reader at the other end is a machine that cannot guess what you meant.

lecture_title: 2.1 - What Human Languages Teach Us About Grammar
text: Look at how English builds meaning in layers. At the bottom you have words, and each word has a category: noun, verb, adjective. Words combine into phrases, like the big dog, which is a noun phrase. Phrases combine into sentences, like the big dog chased a small cat. Notice that a phrase can sit inside another phrase. The cat that the dog chased ran away has a sentence tucked inside a noun phrase. This nesting has no fixed limit, and it is the single most important structural idea we will borrow, because it means a grammar is recursive, and recursive structure is a tree.

lecture_title: 2.1 - What Human Languages Teach Us About Grammar
text: Let me draw that tree. The sentence splits into a noun phrase, the big dog, and a verb phrase, chased a small cat. The verb phrase splits again into the verb chased and another noun phrase. Every branch is a category, and the leaves are the actual words. Linguists call this a parse tree, and when we build Ember's parser, we will produce nearly the same shape for code. So `1 + 2 * 3` will be a tree with an addition at the top, a number on its left, and a multiplication on its right. The structure is what carries the meaning, not the order of the characters alone.

lecture_title: 2.1 - What Human Languages Teach Us About Grammar
text: Here is another lesson. Human grammar can be ambiguous. I saw the man with the telescope. Who has the telescope, me or the man? The words are identical, but there are two different trees. Humans resolve that with context, tone, common sense. A programming language cannot afford that, because a computer has no common sense. So the grammar of a language has to be unambiguous: every valid program must have exactly one tree. That is why we will spend a whole lecture on operator precedence later, to settle what `1 + 2 * 3` means before anyone gets confused.

lecture_title: 2.1 - What Human Languages Teach Us About Grammar
text: Now notice what grammar does not do. Colorless green ideas sleep furiously is a famous sentence by Noam Chomsky. It is perfectly grammatical, the structure is flawless, yet it means nothing. Grammar tells you a sentence is well formed, not whether it is true, sensible, or even possible. Keep that in your pocket. It is the whole difference between syntax and semantics, which is exactly what we dig into in the next lecture. For now, the idea is that checking structure is one job, and giving meaning is a different job, and we will build them as separate pieces.

lecture_title: 2.1 - What Human Languages Teach Us About Grammar
text: Chomsky also gave us a useful tool. He described grammars as sets of rewriting rules: a sentence can be rewritten as a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase, and a noun phrase can be rewritten as a determiner followed by a noun, and so on until you hit real words. We will write Ember's grammar in this style, using a notation called BNF, and each rule will say what something can be rewritten into. So when you write a language grammar, you are doing what linguists do, just with fewer idioms and no sarcasm.

lecture_title: 2.1 - What Human Languages Teach Us About Grammar
text: So let me sum up what we're borrowing. One, words have categories, and in code we will call those token types. Two, words combine into nested phrases, and in code we will call those nodes of a syntax tree. Three, a grammar is a finite set of rules that can generate an unlimited number of valid sentences, thanks to recursion. And four, a good language grammar must be unambiguous. Next lecture we'll put pressure on a question people argue about: is a programming language just its syntax? I'll give you a hint. Absolutely not, okay?

lecture_title: 2.2 - Syntax vs Semantics: Is a Language Just Its Syntax?
text: Here's a question to open with. Take two lines: `x = x + 1` in a language like JavaScript, and `x = x + 1` in a language like Haskell, or a math textbook. The characters are the same. Does it mean the same thing? In math it is nonsense, because no number equals itself plus one. In JavaScript it increments a variable. Same syntax, different semantics. So when somebody says they know a language, they don't mean they memorized what valid code looks like. They mean they know what the code does. Syntax is what a program looks like. Semantics is what it means, and what happens when it runs.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Syntax vs Semantics: Is a Language Just Its Syntax?
text: Let me define each properly. Syntax is the set of rules for which strings of characters count as a valid program, the grammar. If you forget a closing bracket, that's a syntax error, and the language rejects your program before it does anything. Semantics is the set of rules for what a valid program does. When we write `let a = 2 + 3;`, the semantics say: evaluate the right side, get five, and bind the name `a` to that value in the current scope. A syntax error is a failure to be a sentence. A semantic problem is a sentence that says something the language cannot honor.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Syntax vs Semantics: Is a Language Just Its Syntax?
text: Let me give you examples of the second kind. In JavaScript, `undefinedName + 1` is perfectly valid syntax, it's an identifier, a plus and a number. But when it runs, you get a ReferenceError because the name does not exist. That is a runtime semantic error. Some languages catch some of these earlier. A type checker in TypeScript or Java says you cannot add a string to a boolean before the program ever runs. That's a static semantic check. So semantics is not one thing, it can be checked at different moments, and which moment you choose is a major design decision for a language.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Syntax vs Semantics: Is a Language Just Its Syntax?
text: Now let me say something that surprises people. Two languages can share nearly identical syntax and behave completely differently. JavaScript and Java both use curly braces, `if`, `while` and semicolons, but Java is statically typed with classes and JavaScript is dynamic with prototypes. And the opposite also holds: the same semantics can wear different syntax. A loop that counts to ten means the same thing whether you write it with braces, with indentation like Python, or with an `end` keyword like Ruby. The surface can change while the behavior stays the same.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Syntax vs Semantics: Is a Language Just Its Syntax?
text: So is a language just its syntax? No, and this matters for our build. In Ember we will build the syntax side in two stages, the tokenizer and the parser, and neither of them ever executes anything. They only answer: is this a well-formed program, and what is its structure? Then we build the semantics side as the interpreter, which takes the tree and decides what it means. Notice how cleanly the course maps onto the idea. Tokenizer and parser equal syntax. Interpreter equals semantics. If you ever get confused about where a bug lives, ask whether the program is shaped wrong or behaves wrong.

lecture_title: 2.2 - Syntax vs Semantics: Is a Language Just Its Syntax?
text: There's one more subtlety. Semantics has to be specified exactly, or two implementations of the same language drift apart. That's why JavaScript has a formal specification, ECMAScript, with precise steps for what every operation does. For Ember, our specification is simply the interpreter itself, which is common for small languages. Whatever our evaluator does is the meaning. In the next chapter we will list the semantic building blocks that almost every language shares: values, types, variables, scope and control flow. Those are the questions the interpreter will have to answer, so it is worth naming them before we code.

Let's talk about the first building block of any language: values. A value is a piece of data that the language can hold and pass around. The number 42 is a value. The text "hello" is a value. True and false are values. When your program runs, everything it does comes down to producing values, storing them, and handing them to other operations. If you want to understand what a language is, ask what values it has. Ember will have a small set: numbers, strings, booleans, a special value called `nil` meaning nothing, and, importantly, functions.

Each value has a datatype, which says what kind of thing it is and what you can do with it. A number can be added, subtracted and compared. A string can be joined with another string. A boolean drives decisions. The language has to decide what happens when you misuse a type. What is `"5" + 1`? In JavaScript, it quietly becomes the string "51". In Python, it is an error. Ember is going to be strict here: adding a string to a number will raise an error, because I'd rather catch a mistake than silently guess what you meant.

Languages also differ in when types are checked. In a statically typed language like Java, the type of every variable is known before running, and the compiler complains early. In a dynamically typed language like JavaScript, values carry their types around at runtime, and the check happens when the operation executes. Ember is dynamic. A variable has no type at all, only the value currently stored in it has one. That makes our interpreter simpler: each value is just a JavaScript value, and we can inspect it with `typeof` when we need to know what it is.

Next, expressions. An expression is any piece of code that produces a value. `5` is an expression. `2 + 3` is an expression, built from two smaller ones. `add(1, 2)` is an expression that calls a function. The important thing is that expressions nest, so a big expression is made of smaller expressions, which is the tree again. Evaluating an expression means reducing it to a single value. To get `2 + 3 * 4`, you work out the multiplication, get twelve, then the addition, get fourteen. Our interpreter will do exactly this, recursively: evaluate the children, combine the results.

Contrast that with a statement. A statement does something, but it is not asked to produce a value. `let x = 5;` is a statement: it creates a binding. `while` loops and `if` blocks are statements. A program is a sequence of statements, and some of those statements contain expressions. Some languages blur this. In Rust and Ruby, nearly everything is an expression. In JavaScript, you have a clear split, with an expression statement as a bridge, where you write an expression followed by a semicolon just for its effects, like `print(x);`. Ember follows the JavaScript model, and that split will show up in our parser as two separate families of node.

Let's also look at operators, since they are expressions in disguise. An operator like `+` or `==` is just a function with special syntax. It has an arity, meaning how many inputs, with unary taking one, like `-x` or `!ready`, and binary taking two, like `a * b`. It also has a precedence and an associativity, which decide how a chain like `a - b - c` groups. These are grammar questions, and we will answer them carefully in chapter four. For now, remember the pair: values are the nouns of a language, expressions are the phrases that produce them, and statements are the sentences that get things done.

Now variables. A variable is a name bound to a value, so that you can refer to the value later without repeating it. In Ember we write `let total = 10;`, which says: create the name `total` and attach the value ten to it. Later, `total` as an expression looks the name up and gives you the value. And `total = total + 5;` assigns a new value to the same name. Note that there are two operations here, declaring a name with `let`, and assigning to an existing one. Keeping those separate, as JavaScript does, lets us catch typos, because assigning to a name that was never declared can be an error.

Where does a name live? That is the question of scope. Scope is the region of a program where a name is visible. If I declare `let x = 1;` at the top of a file, it is visible everywhere below, it's global. If I declare `let y = 2;` inside a function, it is visible only inside that function. This is lexical scope, also called static scope, meaning the visibility is determined by where the code is written, not by who called it at runtime. JavaScript, Java, Python and C all use lexical scope, and Ember will too.

Scopes nest. A block inside a function can see the function's variables, and the function can see the global ones. When you use a name, the language looks in the innermost scope first. If it's not there, it checks the enclosing one, and keeps going outward until it finds the name or runs out of scopes. This chain of scopes is called the scope chain. If two scopes declare the same name, the inner one shadows the outer one: inside, the inner name wins, outside, the original is untouched. When we build the interpreter, an environment object with a link to its parent will represent exactly this chain.

Then there is control flow, which is how a program decides what to run and how many times. The simplest program runs statement after statement. Conditionals break that: `if (x > 3) { ... } else { ... }` chooses a branch depending on a value. Loops repeat: `while (n > 0) { ... }` keeps going as long as its condition is truthy. And functions create a different kind of jump. A call transfers control into the function body, and `return` transfers it back with a value. These few constructs, branching, repetition, and calling, are enough to express any computation. Truly: a language with just variables, conditionals, loops and functions is Turing complete.

Let me connect these to what we will build. Variables and scope become the environment, in a file I'll call environment.js, or really a class inside interpreter.js, with a `define` method for `let`, an `assign` method for `=`, and a `get` for lookups, all walking up the parent chain. Control flow becomes cases in the evaluator: when we meet an `IfStatement` node, we evaluate the condition and run one branch, and when we meet a `WhileStatement`, we loop in JavaScript. Functions become values that capture the environment where they were created, which gives us closures, for free, with no special machinery.

So here is the full inventory of Ember's semantic parts. Values: numbers, strings, booleans, nil, functions. Expressions: literals, operators, names, calls. Statements: `let`, expression statements, `if`, `while`, `return`, blocks. Scope: lexical, with a chain of environments. That list is the specification we will implement. Nothing more. In the next chapter, we step out of the language itself and look at what happens to code before it runs: how source becomes bytecode and machine code, and what compilers, interpreters and transpilers each do about it.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Machine Code, Bytecode and Your Code
text: So far we have talked about the code you write. Now let's follow that code on its journey to actually running. Start with the bottom of the stack again. The processor executes machine code, which is a stream of binary instructions specific to a processor family, like x86-64 on most laptops or ARM on phones and recent Macs. Machine code is fast because the hardware executes it directly. But it is not portable, because code for ARM means nothing to an x86 chip, and it is not something you would ever want to write by hand.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Machine Code, Bytecode and Your Code
text: Between your source and machine code there is often a middle layer called bytecode. Bytecode is a compact set of instructions for an imaginary machine. Instead of targeting a real processor, you target a virtual one, and then a program called a virtual machine executes those instructions. Java compiles to JVM bytecode, Python compiles to its own bytecode and stores it in those pyc files you sometimes see, and V8 compiles JavaScript to a bytecode called Ignition bytecode before anything else. Bytecode is portable, because any machine with the virtual machine can run it, and it is simpler to run than your original source text.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Machine Code, Bytecode and Your Code
text: Why bother with that middle layer? Think about the work involved. Source code is designed for humans: it has comments, whitespace, long names, nested syntax. Running it directly means constantly re-parsing. Bytecode is flat and numeric, closer to what a loop can chew through quickly, but still independent of the real hardware. So the typical pipeline looks like this: source text, then tokens, then a syntax tree, then bytecode, then either an interpreter loop that executes the bytecode, or a further step that compiles it to native machine code.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Machine Code, Bytecode and Your Code
text: Let me contrast that with Ember. We are skipping the bytecode stage entirely. Our pipeline is source text, tokens, tree, and then we walk the tree directly. That is why we call it a tree-walking interpreter. It is simpler, because there is one fewer representation to design, and it is slower, because walking a tree of JavaScript objects involves many function calls and pointer lookups per operation. For learning, that trade is perfect. And if you ever decide to extend Ember, adding a bytecode compiler would be a natural next project, and you would have all the front-end pieces ready.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Machine Code, Bytecode and Your Code
text: Let me show you what bytecode looks like conceptually, so it isn't mysterious. Take `2 + 3`. A stack-based virtual machine might have instructions like: push 2, push 3, add. The machine keeps a stack. Push puts a number on top. Add pops two numbers, adds them, and pushes the result. That's it. A loop reads one instruction at a time and does a switch on the instruction type. Our tree walker does the same job with recursion: evaluate the left child, evaluate the right child, add. Same computation, different representation. One flattens the tree into a list, the other keeps the tree.

lecture_title: 4.1 - Machine Code, Bytecode and Your Code
text: So now you have a map. Source code is for humans. A tree is for understanding structure. Bytecode is for efficient, portable execution. Machine code is for the hardware. Every language implementation picks a path through these layers, and different paths give different trade-offs between speed, portability, startup time and simplicity. In the next lecture we name the main paths: compilers, interpreters and transpilers, and I'll show you that the difference between them is smaller, and more interesting, than the textbook definitions suggest.

People throw around the words compiler, interpreter and transpiler as if they were totally different animals. They're closer relatives than you'd think, so let me define each one carefully. A compiler translates a program from one language into another, and it does this ahead of running. The classic case is translating a high-level language into machine code, like compiling C with gcc into an executable file. After compilation, the compiler is out of the picture. You just run the output, and it executes directly on the processor with no translator in between.

An interpreter, by contrast, runs the program itself. It reads your source, or the tree built from it, and performs the actions as it goes. There is no separate output file. The interpreter is the thing doing the work, every time you run the program. Ember's interpreter is exactly this: it takes a tree and executes it. The benefit is quick feedback, since there is no build step, and easy portability, since the interpreter is itself just a program. The cost is speed, because the interpretation overhead is paid on every operation.

A transpiler, sometimes called a source-to-source compiler, translates from one high-level language into another high-level language at a similar level. TypeScript to JavaScript is the famous example. So is Babel, which turns modern JavaScript with new syntax into older JavaScript that old browsers understand. A transpiler doesn't produce machine code. Its output is still source text for another tool to run, which means that the transpiler is really just the front half of a compiler, with a different back end bolted on.

Here's the key insight. All three share the same front end. Each one tokenizes, parses into a tree, and understands the program's structure. They differ only in what they do with that tree. A compiler walks the tree and emits machine code, or bytecode. An interpreter walks the tree and performs the actions. A transpiler walks the tree and prints out new source code. So if you learn the front end well, which is most of this course, you can build any of the three by changing the last stage. That's a powerful thing to know.

Real systems also mix them. Java is compiled to bytecode by a compiler, then the bytecode is interpreted by the JVM, and hot parts are compiled again at runtime. Python compiles source to bytecode and then interprets it, so the question of whether Python is compiled or interpreted has the honest answer: both. JavaScript in Node goes through V8, which parses, generates bytecode, interprets it, and compiles frequently used functions to machine code. The labels describe stages, not whole languages. A language itself is neither compiled nor interpreted. An implementation of it is.

Let me make that concrete with Ember. We could write a transpiler that prints Ember as JavaScript, by walking the same tree and emitting strings, where a `FunctionDeclaration` node becomes a `function` declaration. We could write a compiler that emits bytecode. Or, as we do, an interpreter that executes the tree. All start with tokenizer.js and parser.js. That is why those two files matter most. Alright, one more piece of the picture remains: when the translation happens. Ahead of time, or while the program is running? That's the next lecture.

lecture_title: 4.3 - AOT vs JIT: How C++, Java, Python and V8 Run Your Code
text: Let's finish this chapter with the question of timing: when does translation to machine code happen? There are two broad answers. Ahead-of-time, abbreviated AOT, means you translate everything before the program runs. Just-in-time, JIT, means you translate while it runs, using what you learn from watching the program behave. Both are compilation. The difference is the moment, and the information available at that moment. Let's see how four well-known systems answer: C++, Java, Python and V8.

lecture_title: 4.3 - AOT vs JIT: How C++, Java, Python and V8 Run Your Code
text: C++ is the textbook AOT case. You run a compiler such as clang or g++, which parses your code, optimizes heavily, and writes a native executable for a specific operating system and processor. It has all the time in the world, since compilation happens on your machine, not in front of the user. The program then starts instantly and runs at full speed. The costs are long builds, and the binary is tied to one platform. Also the compiler cannot know how the program will actually be used, so it optimizes based on guesses about the code alone.

lecture_title: 4.3 - AOT vs JIT: How C++, Java, Python and V8 Run Your Code
text: Java sits in the middle. The Java compiler, javac, translates source ahead of time into bytecode, which is portable. At runtime the JVM loads this bytecode and starts by interpreting it. While it runs, the JVM profiles which methods are called most. Those hot methods are compiled to native machine code by a JIT compiler, with optimizations based on real behavior. So Java gets portability from the bytecode and speed from the JIT, at the cost of a warm-up period where the program is slower than it will eventually be.

lecture_title: 4.3 - AOT vs JIT: How C++, Java, Python and V8 Run Your Code
text: Python's mainstream implementation, CPython, compiles your source into bytecode and then runs it in a bytecode interpreter loop written in C. Historically it had no JIT, which is a big part of why plain Python is slower than Java or C++ on tight loops. In exchange, it is simple and starts quickly, and it supports very dynamic features. Newer versions of CPython have been adding experimental JIT work, and alternative implementations such as PyPy have used JIT compilation for years, which reminds us again that speed belongs to the implementation, not the language.

lecture_title: 4.3 - AOT vs JIT: How C++, Java, Python and V8 Run Your Code
text: And V8, the engine inside Chrome and Node. It parses JavaScript into a tree, then a component called Ignition generates bytecode and interprets it. V8 watches which functions run often, and which types flow through them. Then a compiler called TurboFan produces optimized machine code for those hot functions, based on assumptions such as this addition always sees numbers. If an assumption later breaks, say a string shows up, V8 throws the optimized code away and falls back to the bytecode. That fallback is called deoptimization. It is a bet the engine makes, then verifies.

lecture_title: 4.3 - AOT vs JIT: How C++, Java, Python and V8 Run Your Code
text: Where does Ember fall in this picture? It's closest to Python's old style, minus even the bytecode: parse once, then execute by walking the tree, with no AOT or JIT at all. That's the right level for learning, because the performance tricks of V8 are optimizations layered over an idea like ours, and without understanding the base idea you can't understand the tricks. You now have the whole landscape. From here on, we stop surveying and start designing. Next chapter: writing down Ember's grammar in BNF, with precedence and associativity built right into the rules.

Time to write Ember's grammar. We'll use a notation called BNF, Backus-Naur Form, or really a lightly relaxed version of it that many people call EBNF. A BNF rule has a name on the left, an arrow, and on the right what that name can be rewritten into. Names in lowercase are non-terminals, meaning they get expanded further. Things in quotes are terminals, the actual tokens that appear in the program. A vertical bar means or. A star means zero or more of the thing before it. Create a file called grammar.txt in the ember folder and let's write it together. The file is documentation, but it will also be our blueprint.

Start at the top. A program is a list of declarations followed by the end of the file. So: `program -> declaration* EOF`. A declaration is one of three things: a function declaration, a variable declaration, or a plain statement. We write `declaration -> fnDecl | letDecl | statement`. Why separate declarations from statements? Because some places, like the body of an `if` without braces, should allow a statement but not a declaration. It makes `if (x) let y = 1;` illegal, which is good, because that variable would be pointless. This tiny design choice is exactly the kind of thing a grammar lets you decide cleanly.

Now the declarations. A variable declaration is `letDecl -> "let" IDENT ( "=" expression )? ";"`. The question mark means optional, so `let x;` is allowed, and gives `nil`. A function declaration is `fnDecl -> "fn" IDENT "(" parameters? ")" block`, where `parameters -> IDENT ( "," IDENT )*`. So `fn add(a, b) { return a + b; }` fits. Notice IDENT in capitals. That's a terminal category, meaning any identifier token. We will define what counts as an identifier in the tokenizer chapter. Here, the grammar only cares about the token's kind, not its spelling.

Next, statements. `statement -> exprStmt | ifStmt | whileStmt | returnStmt | block`. An expression statement is just `expression ";"`, which is how `print(x);` works. An if statement is `"if" "(" expression ")" statement ( "else" statement )?`. A while statement is `"while" "(" expression ")" statement`. A return statement is `"return" expression? ";"`. And a block is `"{" declaration* "}"`, which is a list of declarations inside braces. See how block refers back to declaration, and declaration refers down to statement, which refers back to block. That circle is recursion, and it is what allows blocks inside blocks forever.

Let me pause on a design decision. Ember requires parentheses around the condition of an `if` or `while`, and requires a semicolon after each simple statement. Some languages make these optional, but optional syntax makes the grammar and the parser harder, and it creates ambiguity. We want the first version of Ember to be boring and strict. Boring grammars are easy to parse with a hand-written recursive-descent parser, which is what we will build later. Python's significant indentation, or JavaScript's automatic semicolon insertion, are real features that cost real implementation complexity. We are not paying that bill today.

So the statement part is done. The expression part is where grammars get interesting, and it is a lecture of its own, so let me only set the stage. `expression -> assignment`, and from there we go down through levels, each handling one kind of operator, until we reach the tightest things such as numbers and parentheses. Each level refers only to the level beneath it, and that ordering is what will encode operator precedence. We'll write all of those rules in the next lecture, and then we'll see how the same structure also fixes associativity, which means which way a chain of equal operators groups.

Let me also list Ember's lexical vocabulary, because the grammar quotes these words. Keywords: `let`, `fn`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false`, `nil`, `and`, `or`. Operators: plus, minus, star, slash, percent, bang, the comparison operators, double equals, bang equals, and a single equals for assignment. Punctuation: parentheses, braces, comma, semicolon. Literals: numbers and double-quoted strings. Comments start with two slashes and run to the end of the line. Anything else is an error. Write that vocabulary at the top of grammar.txt. It's the contract the tokenizer must satisfy.

Before moving on, test your grammar by hand, the way a parser would. Take `let n = 3;`. Program expands to one declaration. That's a letDecl: the word `let`, an identifier `n`, an equals sign, an expression, a semicolon. The expression, after descending through the levels, is the number three. Now try `fn f() { return 1; }`. The parts line up too. If you can derive a program from the grammar, it is syntactically valid, and the derivation itself is the tree. When a program fails to derive, that is a syntax error, and a good parser can tell you where it got stuck. Next lecture, expressions.

Now the expression grammar, and the place where precedence and associativity come to life. Precedence decides which operator binds tighter. In `1 + 2 * 3`, multiplication has higher precedence, so it groups as `1 + (2 * 3)`, which is seven, not nine. Associativity decides how operators of the same level group. In `10 - 4 - 3`, subtraction is left-associative, so it groups as `(10 - 4) - 3`, which is three. If it were right-associative, we'd get `10 - (4 - 3)`, which is nine. Different answers, so the grammar must settle this precisely.

Here's the trick that makes grammars encode precedence: build one rule per precedence level, stacked from loosest at the top to tightest at the bottom. Each rule is defined in terms of the next, tighter one. The loosest operations are assignment, then `or`, then `and`, then equality, comparison, addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, unary operators, calls, and finally primary things like numbers. Open grammar.txt and let's write them, one level at a time. Because tight operators sit deeper in the tree, they get evaluated first, and that is the entire mechanism.

Start from the bottom, which is the easiest. `primary -> NUMBER | STRING | "true" | "false" | "nil" | IDENT | "(" expression ")" | fnExpr`, where `fnExpr -> "fn" "(" parameters? ")" block`. Those are the atoms. Parentheses let you restart at the top, so inside them, anything goes. That is how parentheses override precedence: they jump back to `expression`. Above it, calls: `call -> primary ( "(" arguments? ")" )*`, with `arguments -> expression ( "," expression )*`. The star means you can chain calls like `f(1)(2)`, which matters, because functions can return functions.

Now unary: `unary -> ( "!" | "-" ) unary | call`. Notice the rule refers to itself on the right side, so `- - 5` and `!!ready` both work. That is right recursion, and it makes unary operators right-associative, which is what you want, since they apply from the inside out. Above unary, multiplication: `factor -> unary ( ( "*" | "/" | "%" ) unary )*`. This reads: one unary, followed by any number of operator and unary pairs. The star, instead of a recursive rule, is how we express left associativity: it's a flat sequence that the parser will fold from the left.

Same shape again for the next levels. `term -> factor ( ( "+" | "-" ) factor )*`. `comparison -> term ( ( "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=" ) term )*`. `equality -> comparison ( ( "==" | "!=" ) comparison )*`. Do you see the pattern? Every binary level is: the next tighter level, then zero or more pairs of an operator from this level and the next tighter level again. The only thing that changes is which operators belong. Because term refers to factor, multiplication always lives deeper than addition, so `1 + 2 * 3` can only parse one way, with the multiplication nested inside the addition.

The logical operators follow suit. `logicAnd -> equality ( "and" equality )*` and `logicOr -> logicAnd ( "or" logicAnd )*`. Since `and` is tighter than `or`, `a or b and c` means `a or (b and c)`, just like in JavaScript with `||` and `&&`. They're their own level, and not lumped in with the arithmetic ones, because later the interpreter will treat them differently: they short-circuit, which means the right side might never be evaluated at all.

And at the top, assignment, which is the one right-associative binary operator. `assignment -> IDENT "=" assignment | logicOr`. Here the rule calls itself on the right, so `a = b = 5` means `a = (b = 5)`: assign five to b, and the result, five, to a. Expression, then, is simply `expression -> assignment`. That completes the grammar. Take a minute, hand-derive `a = 1 + 2 * 3` through the levels. You should see assignment, then down through term and factor, with the multiplication deepest. Next chapter, we turn the first half of this into code: the tokenizer.

Welcome to the first code chapter. Everything so far was design. Now we build tokenizer.js, the first stage of the pipeline. Before typing anything, let's get the vocabulary right, because three similar words get mixed up constantly: lexeme, token and token type. A lexeme is the actual slice of text from the source, like `while` or `42` or `+`. A token type is the category the lexeme belongs to, like KEYWORD, NUMBER, or OPERATOR. A token is the object that bundles them together, usually with the type, the lexeme, and a line number for error messages. Lexemes are raw text. Tokens are structured data.

Why do we need this stage at all? Because parsing is hard enough without worrying about whitespace, comments and whether `12` is two characters or a number. The tokenizer, also called the lexer or the scanner, handles all of that, and hands the parser a clean list. Think of reading this sentence: you don't process letters individually, you recognize words first. The tokenizer is the word recognizer. Given `let x = 12 + y;`, it produces the tokens: let, x, equals, twelve, plus, y, semicolon. The whitespace vanishes, and each piece knows what it is.

Let's decide Ember's token types. NUMBER for numeric literals like `3` or `4.5`. STRING for double-quoted text. IDENT for names such as `total` or `makeCounter`. KEYWORD for the reserved words: `let`, `fn`, `if`, `else`, `while`, `return`, `true`, `false`, `nil`, `and` and `or`. OP for the operators, one or two characters long. PUNCT for parentheses, braces, comma and semicolon. And EOF, a special token at the very end, so that the parser always has something to look at and never runs off the array. That's seven types, and every Ember program tokenizes into a sequence of them.

Now let me open tokenizer.js and create the shape. Each token is a plain object, so we'll make a helper: `function makeToken(type, value, line) { return { type, value, line }; }`. For a number, the value is the JavaScript number, so `42` becomes `{ type: 'NUMBER', value: 42, line: 1 }`. For an identifier, the value is the name as a string. Keeping the line number in each token costs nothing now, and it pays off when the parser needs to say "unexpected token on line 7". Error messages are what separate a toy from a tool, so we'll thread line numbers through from the start.

Let me define the keyword set, since the identifier code will use it. At the top of the file: `const KEYWORDS = new Set(['let', 'fn', 'if', 'else', 'while', 'return', 'true', 'false', 'nil', 'and', 'or']);`. Why a Set? Because we'll ask "is this word a keyword?" for every identifier, and a Set answers in constant time. Here's the important idea: the tokenizer doesn't scan for keywords separately. It scans a word, as if it were an identifier, and then checks the set. If the word is in it, the type becomes KEYWORD, otherwise IDENT. That way `letter` is correctly an identifier, because the whole word is `letter`, not `let`.

There is a classic rule behind that, called maximal munch: always take the longest lexeme that matches. When the tokenizer sees `letter`, it keeps consuming letters until the word ends, and only then decides what it is. Same for operators: when it sees `=`, it has to peek at the next character. If that's another `=`, then the lexeme is `==`, not two assignments. If it sees `<` followed by `=`, we get `<=`. Without maximal munch, `a <= b` would be tokenized as `a < = b`, and the parser would fall over. Keep that rule in mind, because we will use it for numbers and operators in the next lecture.

Last thing before we code the loop. What does the tokenizer do with things it doesn't understand, like an `@` or a stray `#`? It should fail loudly and helpfully. We'll throw an Error with a message like `Unexpected character '@' on line 3`. Not skip it, not guess. A language that quietly ignores junk hides bugs. We'll export a single function from this file, `tokenize(source)`, that takes a string and returns an array of tokens ending with EOF. In the next lecture, we write the loop that makes it work, one character at a time.

Let's write the loop. Open tokenizer.js, below the keyword set and makeToken. The function is `function tokenize(source) {`, and inside we need three pieces of state. `const tokens = [];` for the output, `let pos = 0;` for where we are in the string, and `let line = 1;` for error messages. The core idea is a `while (pos < source.length)` loop. On each pass, we look at the current character, decide what kind of lexeme starts here, consume it, push a token if there is one, and go around again. Every branch must advance `pos`, or we'd loop forever, so that's the thing to watch.

First branch: whitespace. Inside the loop, `const ch = source[pos];`. If `ch` is a newline, we do `line++` and `pos++`, and `continue`. If it is a space, a tab, or a carriage return, we just `pos++` and continue. Whitespace produces no token, which is why the parser never has to think about it. Second branch: comments. If `ch === '/'` and `source[pos + 1] === '/'`, we skip forward until we hit a newline or the end, with `while (pos < source.length && source[pos] !== '\n') pos++;`. We deliberately don't consume the newline itself, so that the whitespace branch counts the line.

Third branch: numbers. If the character is a digit, we want the whole number. I'll write a small helper, `function isDigit(c) { return c >= '0' && c <= '9'; }`. Then we record `const start = pos;`, advance while digits continue, and then check for a decimal point: if the current character is a dot and the one after it is a digit, consume the dot and the fractional digits. Why peek beyond the dot? So that something like `3.` followed by a letter doesn't get glued together. Finally the lexeme is `source.slice(start, pos)`, and we push `makeToken('NUMBER', Number(text), line)`. Notice we convert to a real JavaScript number here, so later stages never parse text again.

Fourth: identifiers and keywords. A name starts with a letter or an underscore, and continues with letters, digits or underscores. Two helpers: `isAlpha` and `isAlphaNumeric`. Then, same pattern: remember `start`, advance while the character is alphanumeric, slice the text. Now the keyword check we talked about: `const type = KEYWORDS.has(text) ? 'KEYWORD' : 'IDENT';` and push `makeToken(type, text, line)`. That's maximal munch in action, since we consumed the entire word before deciding. Notice how little code this is. A tokenizer looks intimidating from the outside, but it's mostly a handful of small branches like this.

Fifth: strings. If the character is a double quote, we advance past it, then collect characters until the closing quote. `const start = ++pos;` then `while (pos < source.length && source[pos] !== '"') { if (source[pos] === '\n') line++; pos++; }`. If we hit the end of the file without a closing quote, we throw `Unterminated string on line N`. Otherwise the value is `source.slice(start, pos)`, we step past the closing quote with `pos++`, and push a STRING token. For now there are no escape sequences. A string can't contain a double quote. That's a limitation we accept so the tokenizer stays short, and you can add escapes as an exercise.

Sixth: operators and punctuation. For single-character punctuation, one set check: `'(){},;'.includes(ch)` produces a PUNCT token. For operators, we handle the two-character ones first, using lookahead. A helper `const two = source.slice(pos, pos + 2);` and then `if (['==', '!=', '<=', '>='].includes(two))` we push an OP token with that value, and do `pos += 2`. Only if that fails do we check the single-character operators, `'+-*/%<>=!'`, push the OP, and `pos++`. Order matters here. If we checked the single characters first, we'd never see the doubles. That is maximal munch again, longest match first.

Finally, the fallback: if no branch matched, `throw new Error(`Unexpected character '${ch}' on line ${line}`);`. And after the loop ends, push the sentinel: `tokens.push(makeToken('EOF', null, line));` and `return tokens;`. At the bottom, `module.exports = { tokenize };`. Let's test it right in the terminal. `node -e "console.log(require('./tokenizer').tokenize('let x = 12 + y;'))"`. You should get seven tokens plus EOF, with `let` typed KEYWORD, `x` typed IDENT, `=` typed OP, and the number as a real number. Try a string, a comment, and an `@` for the error path.

One last idea before we move on: the tokenizer we just wrote is a hand-written state machine, with the branches deciding what state to enter based on the first character. Tools like lex and flex generate this from patterns, and many JavaScript tools use regular expressions. Hand-writing it, as we did, gives us the best error messages and total control, and it's only about eighty lines. We now have the first half of syntax done: raw text becomes a flat list of typed tokens. But a flat list has no structure, and that's the parser's job. Next chapter, we build parser.js and grow the tree.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Now we build the part of the course that most people find magical: the parser. We have an array of tokens, flat and in order. We want a tree. Recursive descent is the simplest way to do it, and it's what many real compilers use, including the ones inside V8 and GCC. The idea is wonderfully direct: write one function for each rule in the grammar, and let those functions call each other the same way the rules refer to each other. The grammar is the design, and the code is almost a transliteration of it. If you wrote grammar.txt carefully, then half of the work is already done.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Create parser.js. First the plumbing. `class Parser { constructor(tokens) { this.tokens = tokens; this.current = 0; } }`. The `current` field is the index of the next token to consume. We need a handful of tiny helpers. `peek()` returns `this.tokens[this.current]` without consuming it. `advance()` returns that token and moves forward. `check(type, value)` asks whether the next token has a given type, and optionally a given value. `match(type, value)` checks, and if it matches, advances and returns true. And `expect(type, value, message)` demands a token, and throws an error with the line number if it's not there. These five helpers are the entire vocabulary of the parser.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Let me write the helpers properly. `check(type, value) { const t = this.peek(); return t.type === type && (value === undefined || t.value === value); }`. Then `match(type, value) { if (this.check(type, value)) { this.advance(); return true; } return false; }`. And `expect(type, value, message) { if (this.check(type, value)) return this.advance(); throw new Error(`${message} on line ${this.peek().line}`); }`. That last helper is where good error messages come from. When the parser fails, it knows exactly what it wanted, and the line of what it found instead.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Let's start at the bottom of the expression grammar, because the lowest rule is the easiest. `primary()`. If we `match('NUMBER')`, we return a node `{ type: 'Literal', value }` using the token we just consumed. I'll grab it with `const tok = this.advance()` after checking. Same for STRING. For the keywords `true`, `false` and `nil`, we return Literal nodes with `true`, `false` and `null`. For an IDENT, we return `{ type: 'Identifier', name: tok.value }`. And if we see an open parenthesis, we advance, call `this.expression()`, then `expect('PUNCT', ')', "Expected ')'")`, and return the inner expression directly. Parentheses vanish from the tree. They only existed to guide the parse.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Here is the key part. How do the binary levels work in code? Remember the grammar: `term -> factor ( ( "+" | "-" ) factor )*`. In code, that's a loop. `term() { let left = this.factor(); while (this.check('OP', '+') || this.check('OP', '-')) { const operator = this.advance().value; const right = this.factor(); left = { type: 'Binary', operator, left, right }; } return left; }`. Read it slowly. We parse one factor. Then as long as a plus or minus follows, we parse another factor, and wrap what we have so far as the left child of a new Binary node. That wrapping is exactly what makes it left-associative.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Let me trace `10 - 4 - 3`. We parse 10 as the first factor, so left is Literal ten. We see minus, parse 4, and build Binary(10 - 4). The loop continues, we see another minus, parse 3, and build Binary(Binary(10 - 4) - 3). The older node became the left child of the newer one. That tree evaluates to three, as left associativity demands. If I had written the recursion the other way, with the right side calling `term()` again, I'd have gotten the nine. So a loop is left-associative, and right recursion is right-associative. That one distinction explains all associativity, and now you've seen it in code.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Now the remaining binary levels are copy and paste with different names. To avoid repeating myself, I'll write a helper: `binaryLevel(next, operators) { let left = next.call(this); while (operators.some(op => this.check('OP', op))) { const operator = this.advance().value; const right = next.call(this); left = { type: 'Binary', operator, left, right }; } return left; }`. Then `factor() { return this.binaryLevel(this.unary, ['*', '/', '%']); }`, `term()` uses factor with plus and minus, `comparison()` uses term with the four comparison operators, and `equality()` uses comparison with double equals and bang equals. The structure of the grammar is now just a table.

lecture_title: 7.1 - Recursive Descent: Turning Tokens into a Tree
text: Then the three unusual ones. `unary()`: if we match a `!` or `-` operator, we take it, call `this.unary()` recursively, and return `{ type: 'Unary', operator, operand }`. Otherwise we return `this.call()`. `call()`: parse a primary, then `while (this.match('PUNCT', '('))` collect arguments separated by commas until the closing parenthesis, and wrap in `{ type: 'Call', callee, args }`. Logical `or` and `and` are the same loop shape, but they produce `{ type: 'Logical', operator, left, right }` nodes, since the interpreter will short-circuit them. And `assignment()` parses a `logicOr()` first, and if an equals sign follows, and the left side is an Identifier, it recurses to get the value and returns an Assign node. Otherwise it throws "Invalid assignment target". Next, statements.

With expressions done, statements are almost relaxing. Statements in the grammar are mostly keyword-led: the first token tells you which rule you're in, so there is no guessing. That property is what makes recursive descent work so cleanly here, we decide using one token of lookahead. Open parser.js and add the entry point. `parse() { const body = []; while (!this.check('EOF')) body.push(this.declaration()); return { type: 'Program', body }; }`. The tree's root is a Program node with a list of statements. And `declaration()` is the dispatcher: if the next token is the keyword `let`, we go to `letDeclaration`, if it is `fn` and the token after it is an identifier, to `fnDeclaration`, otherwise to `statement`. So the dispatcher peeks one token past `fn`, and `fn` followed by an open parenthesis falls through to expression parsing.

Let's do `letDeclaration()`. We've already seen the keyword by the time we get here, so we `this.advance()` past it. Then `const name = this.expect('IDENT', undefined, 'Expected variable name').value;`. Then `let init = null; if (this.match('OP', '=')) init = this.expression();`. Then `this.expect('PUNCT', ';', "Expected ';' after variable declaration");`. We return `{ type: 'LetStatement', name, init }`. I'll point out that every `expect` includes a message of what was missing. When you test the parser with broken programs, those messages are the user interface, so write them like you'd want to read them.

Now statements. `statement()` looks at the next token. If it's the keyword `if`, `while` or `return`, we call the matching method. If it's an opening brace, we parse a block. Otherwise it must be an expression statement. `ifStatement()`: advance past `if`, expect `(`, parse the condition with `this.expression()`, expect `)`. Then `const consequent = this.statement();`, and `let alternate = null; if (this.match('KEYWORD', 'else')) alternate = this.statement();`. We return `{ type: 'IfStatement', test, consequent, alternate }`. The else branch is optional because we check for it rather than demand it. That's where the dangling else gets resolved: an else attaches to the nearest if, since the inner call grabs it first.

`whileStatement()` has the same shape: advance, expect parentheses around the expression, then `const body = this.statement();`, returning `{ type: 'WhileStatement', test, body }`. For `returnStatement()`, we advance past `return`, and then `let value = null; if (!this.check('PUNCT', ';')) value = this.expression();`, expect a semicolon, and return `{ type: 'ReturnStatement', value }`. So a bare `return;` is allowed, and gives nil. The expression statement is simplest of all: `const expr = this.expression(); this.expect('PUNCT', ';', "Expected ';' after expression"); return { type: 'ExpressionStatement', expression: expr };`.

Blocks. When we see `{`, we advance, then collect declarations until we reach `}`. `block() { this.expect('PUNCT', '{', "Expected '{'"); const body = []; while (!this.check('PUNCT', '}') && !this.check('EOF')) body.push(this.declaration()); this.expect('PUNCT', '}', "Expected '}'"); return { type: 'BlockStatement', body }; }`. The check for EOF stops an unterminated block from looping forever, and lets the final `expect` produce a proper error. Blocks call `declaration`, not `statement`, so you can declare variables inside them, and that nesting is what produces nested scopes later on in the interpreter.

Finally functions. A function declaration: advance past `fn`, expect an identifier for the name, expect `(`, then parameters. `const params = []; if (!this.check('PUNCT', ')')) { do { params.push(this.expect('IDENT', undefined, 'Expected parameter name').value); } while (this.match('PUNCT', ',')); } this.expect('PUNCT', ')', "Expected ')' after parameters");`. Then `const body = this.block();`, and we return `{ type: 'FunctionDeclaration', name, params, body }`. A function expression is the same without a name, and lives in `primary`: when we see `fn` followed by `(`, we build `{ type: 'FunctionExpression', params, body }`. Since the dispatcher peeks one token past `fn`, a declaration is `fn` followed by a name, while `fn` followed by a parenthesis falls through to expression parsing. That's how `fn() {}` can be a value.

Let me put it together and test. In the terminal, run `node -e "const {tokenize}=require('./tokenizer'); const {Parser}=require('./parser'); console.log(JSON.stringify(new Parser(tokenize('fn add(a, b) { return a + b; } let r = add(1, 2 * 3);')).parse(), null, 1))"`. You should get a Program with two entries: a FunctionDeclaration whose body block holds a ReturnStatement of a Binary, and a LetStatement whose init is a Call, with the second argument as Binary multiplication. That's the tree the whole language hangs on. The syntax half is finished. Next chapter, we write interpreter.js and make this tree do something.

Now we give the tree meaning. This is the semantics half of the course, and it lives in interpreter.js. The idea of a tree-walking evaluator is simple enough to say in one sentence: for each kind of node, write the rule for what it does, and when a node contains other nodes, evaluate those first by calling yourself. That is recursion again, and it mirrors the tree exactly. The parser went from the flat list down into nested structure. The interpreter goes through the nested structure and collapses it back down to values. So let's create the class. `class Interpreter { constructor() { this.globals = new Environment(); } }`. We'll write Environment in the next lecture, so for now just treat it as a place to store names.

We need two main methods, matching the two families of node we made. `evaluate(node, env)` handles expressions and returns a value. `execute(node, env)` handles statements, and returns nothing in general. Each of them is one big `switch (node.type)`. I like to start with the simplest case and build up. In `evaluate`, `case 'Literal': return node.value;`. That's it. A literal evaluates to itself. If you run nothing else yet, `evaluate({ type: 'Literal', value: 5 })` gives five, and that's a working interpreter for a language with one construct. It's worth enjoying that. Everything from here is just adding cases.

Next, grouping is gone already because the parser dropped parentheses. So the next case is unary. `case 'Unary': { const operand = this.evaluate(node.operand, env); if (node.operator === '-') { this.checkNumber(node.operator, operand); return -operand; } if (node.operator === '!') return !this.isTruthy(operand); }`. Look at the order: we evaluate the child first, then apply the operator. That's post-order traversal, children before parent. I introduced two helpers. `isTruthy(value)` returns false for `false` and for `null`, which is how we represent nil, and true for everything else. And `checkNumber` throws a runtime error if the operand isn't a number.

Let me show those helpers. `isTruthy(v) { return !(v === null || v === false); }`. Notice that in Ember, zero and the empty string are truthy. I made that choice to avoid the surprising rules JavaScript has around falsy values. Only `false` and `nil` are false. `checkNumber(operator, ...values) { for (const v of values) if (typeof v !== 'number') throw new Error(`Operand of '${operator}' must be a number`); }`. Real languages attach line numbers to runtime errors too. If you want that, add `line` to the nodes in the parser from the tokens, and include it here as an extension later.

Now binary expressions, which is where evaluation really shows. `case 'Binary': { const left = this.evaluate(node.left, env); const right = this.evaluate(node.right, env); switch (node.operator) { ... } }`. For `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, we call `checkNumber` and compute in JavaScript. For `/` we also check that the right side isn't zero, and throw "Division by zero". For `+`, we allow two numbers or two strings, otherwise throw "Operands of '+' must be two numbers or two strings". Comparison operators need numbers. Equality, `==` and `!=`, works on any values, and we use JavaScript's `===`, so there's no coercion: five is never equal to the string five.

Take a moment to appreciate how the tree handles precedence now. Recall that `1 + 2 * 3` parsed to a Binary plus with a Literal one on the left and a Binary times on the right. Our evaluator evaluates the left, getting one. Evaluates the right, which recursively evaluates two and three and multiplies them into six. Then adds to seven. We never wrote one line of precedence logic in the interpreter. The tree shape already carries it. That's the payoff for doing the grammar carefully: the later stages are almost mechanical. Parentheses, associativity, all of it is already encoded in the structure we receive.

Logical operators are different, because they short-circuit. `case 'Logical': { const left = this.evaluate(node.left, env); if (node.operator === 'or') { if (this.isTruthy(left)) return left; } else { if (!this.isTruthy(left)) return left; } return this.evaluate(node.right, env); }`. We only evaluate the right side if we need to. So `false and boom()` never calls boom. Note too that we return the actual operand and not a boolean, just like JavaScript, so `nil or "default"` gives "default", a handy idiom. This is why we separated Logical from Binary in the parser: they need different evaluation rules, and the tree remembers which is which.

We can also add `execute` for the simplest statements. `case 'ExpressionStatement': this.evaluate(node.expression, env); break;` and `case 'Program'` loops over the body. To see output we need a way to print, and we'll provide it as a native function in a moment. For now, you can test by returning the value of a single expression. Write `new Interpreter().evaluate(new Parser(tokenize('1 + 2 * 3')).expression(), env)` and see seven come out. That's the whole pipeline working: text, tokens, tree, value. Next lecture, we make names work, through environments, which is where scoping, hoisting and closures finally come to life.

Names now. When the evaluator meets an Identifier node, it has to find the value bound to that name. Where is it stored? In an environment. An environment is a table of name to value, plus a link to the enclosing environment, which is its parent. That link is the scope chain from chapter two, made real. Let's create environment.js. `class Environment { constructor(parent = null) { this.values = new Map(); this.parent = parent; } }`. A Map is perfect, since the keys are names. And global scope is simply an Environment whose parent is null.

Three methods. `define(name, value) { this.values.set(name, value); }` creates or overwrites a name in this very environment, which is what `let` does. `get(name)` looks up the chain: `if (this.values.has(name)) return this.values.get(name); if (this.parent) return this.parent.get(name); throw new Error(`Undefined variable '${name}'`);`. And `assign(name, value)` finds the nearest environment that already has the name and updates it there, and throws if it reaches the top without finding it. The difference between define and assign is the difference between `let x = 1;` and `x = 1;`, and it decides which variable you're touching.

Let's plug it into the interpreter. `case 'Identifier': return env.get(node.name);`. `case 'Assign': { const value = this.evaluate(node.value, env); env.assign(node.name, value); return value; }`. And in `execute`, `case 'LetStatement': { const value = node.init ? this.evaluate(node.init, env) : null; env.define(node.name, value); break; }`. Try it: `let x = 5; x = x + 1;` and then look at the global environment, you'll find x as six. We can also seed the globals with a native `print`: `this.globals.define('print', { native: true, call: (args) => console.log(...args) })`. We'll teach calls about that shape soon.

Next, blocks and scope. `case 'BlockStatement': this.executeBlock(node.body, new Environment(env)); break;`. A block creates a fresh child environment, whose parent is the current one, and runs its statements there. When the block finishes, we simply discard that environment. So `let y = 2;` inside a block disappears after it. And because lookups walk up the parent links, the block can still read outer variables. Try shadowing: `let a = 1; { let a = 2; print(a); } print(a);` prints two, then one. The inner define landed in the child environment, and never touched the outer one.

Now the interesting one, hoisting. In JavaScript you can call a function before its declaration appears in the source, because function declarations are hoisted. We'll give Ember that same behavior, and it takes about five lines. `executeBlock(statements, env) { for (const s of statements) { if (s.type === 'FunctionDeclaration') env.define(s.name, new EmberFunction(s, env)); } for (const s of statements) { if (s.type !== 'FunctionDeclaration') this.execute(s, env); } }`. A first pass defines every function in the block. A second pass runs everything else. So you can write a call at the top of the file and the function at the bottom, and it works.

And what about `let`? It is not hoisted. If you do `print(x); let x = 5;`, then at the time of the print, x isn't defined, so `get` throws "Undefined variable 'x'". That matches the intuition that a variable exists from the point of its declaration onward. JavaScript has this middle ground called the temporal dead zone, which is a more subtle behavior, but for Ember we use the straightforward rule: functions are hoisted, variables are not. Whenever you design a language, small rules like this are choices. Ours produces predictable behavior and the code is easy to explain, which is the goal.

Now closures. Look at the line `new EmberFunction(s, env)`. We pass the current environment into the function object. That is the closure: a function plus the environment where it was created. `class EmberFunction { constructor(declaration, closure) { this.params = declaration.params; this.body = declaration.body; this.closure = closure; } }`. Later, when the function is called, the new call environment will have `this.closure` as its parent, and not the environment of the caller. That's lexical scope, precisely. A function remembers the variables around where it was written, even if it escapes. So `makeCounter` can return an inner function that still sees its `n`, long after makeCounter returned. We'll see that run in the next lecture.

lecture_title: 8.3 - Running Conditionals, Loops and Function Calls
text: Let's finish the interpreter with control flow and calls. Conditionals first, since they're quick. `case 'IfStatement': { if (this.isTruthy(this.evaluate(node.test, env))) { this.execute(node.consequent, env); } else if (node.alternate) { this.execute(node.alternate, env); } break; }`. Evaluate the test, check truthiness, run one branch. Remember the grammar said the branch is a statement, which usually is a block, and blocks create their own scope, so a variable declared inside the branch doesn't leak out. Only one of the two branches ever runs, and that's all an `if` is. It's just a case in a switch statement in JavaScript.

lecture_title: 8.3 - Running Conditionals, Loops and Function Calls
text: Loops are just as direct. `case 'WhileStatement': { while (this.isTruthy(this.evaluate(node.test, env))) { this.execute(node.body, env); } break; }`. We use a JavaScript while loop to implement Ember's while loop. Each time around, we re-evaluate the test, because the test is an expression in the tree, and the body may have changed a variable. Here is a nice thing to notice: our language borrows the host language's control flow to implement its own. That is a common pattern in interpreters. The cost is that deep recursion in Ember uses the JavaScript call stack, so a runaway recursion becomes a JavaScript stack overflow, which we can catch and report.

lecture_title: 8.3 - Running Conditionals, Loops and Function Calls
text: Now function calls, the most complex piece, so let's go slowly. `case 'Call': { const callee = this.evaluate(node.callee, env); const args = node.args.map(a => this.evaluate(a, env)); return this.callFunction(callee, args); }`. We evaluate the thing being called, which is usually an identifier that looks up a function value, then evaluate each argument in order, then perform the call. Evaluating arguments before the call is called eager or strict evaluation, and it's what JavaScript does. Because the callee is an expression too, `f(1)(2)` works naturally: the outer call's callee is itself a Call.

lecture_title: 8.3 - Running Conditionals, Loops and Function Calls
text: Then `callFunction(fn, args)`. If `fn.native`, we return `fn.call(args)`. That's how `print` works. If it's not an `EmberFunction`, we throw `Can only call functions`. We also check arity: `if (args.length !== fn.params.length) throw new Error(`Expected ${fn.params.length} arguments but got ${args.length}`);`. Then the heart of it. `const callEnv = new Environment(fn.closure); fn.params.forEach((p, i) => callEnv.define(p, args[i]));`. Each call gets a brand new environment, which is why recursion works: every invocation has its own set of parameters, no sharing, and its parent is the closure environment, which makes lexical scope work.

lecture_title: 8.3 - Running Conditionals, Loops and Function Calls
text: Next is return. A `return` can happen deep inside nested blocks and loops, and we need to unwind all the way back to the call. The simplest tool is an exception. `class ReturnSignal { constructor(value) { this.value = value; } }`. In `execute`, `case 'ReturnStatement': throw new ReturnSignal(node.value ? this.evaluate(node.value, env) : null);`. And in `callFunction`: `try { this.executeBlock(fn.body.body, callEnv); } catch (e) { if (e instanceof ReturnSignal) return e.value; throw e; } return null;`. If the function finishes without returning, the result is nil. Notice that ReturnSignal is not an Error. It's control flow, so we rethrow anything that is not ours.

lecture_title: 8.3 - Running Conditionals, Loops and Function Calls
text: Also, function expressions are values: `case 'FunctionExpression': return new EmberFunction(node, env);`. And function declarations are handled by the hoisting pass, and ignored in the main pass. Let's now test the famous closure program. Write `fn makeCounter() { let n = 0; return fn() { n = n + 1; return n; }; } let c = makeCounter(); print(c()); print(c()); print(c());` and run it. You should see one, two, three. The returned function carries makeCounter's environment with it, so `n` survives. It's one of the most powerful ideas in programming, and you built it with about a dozen lines. Next chapter: a real program, end to end.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: Time to put the three stages together and run a real Ember program. First, a runner. Create ember.js in the project folder. It needs to read a file path from the command line, read the file, and push the text through the pipeline. `const fs = require('fs'); const { tokenize } = require('./tokenizer'); const { Parser } = require('./parser'); const { Interpreter } = require('./interpreter');`. Then `const source = fs.readFileSync(process.argv[2], 'utf8'); const tokens = tokenize(source); const program = new Parser(tokens).parse(); new Interpreter().run(program);`. Four lines, one per stage. And in the interpreter, `run(program) { this.executeBlock(program.body, this.globals); }`, so the top level gets hoisting too.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: We should wrap that in a try and catch, so users see friendly messages rather than a JavaScript stack trace. `try { ... } catch (e) { console.error(`Ember error: ${e.message}`); process.exit(1); }`. Our syntax errors from the tokenizer and parser, and runtime errors from the interpreter, are all plain Error objects with readable messages, so one handler covers every stage. This is the benefit of throwing errors at the exact spot where the problem is detected. Test it with a broken file later, since checking the failure paths is how you find out whether your error messages are any good.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: Now let's write the program. Make a file called fib.ember. I'd like something that uses most of the language. First a recursive function: `fn fib(n) { if (n < 2) { return n; } return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }`. Then a loop to print the first ten values: `let i = 0; while (i < 10) { print(fib(i)); i = i + 1; }`. Run it with `node ember.js fib.ember`. You should see zero, one, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, twenty-one, thirty-four. Think about what just happened. Every one of those lines went through your tokenizer, your parser and your interpreter, and nothing else.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: Let's add the closure example and make it richer. Below that: `fn makeCounter() { let n = 0; return fn() { n = n + 1; return n; }; } let a = makeCounter(); let b = makeCounter(); print(a()); print(a()); print(b());`.
