Predict the output before you run it. a's first call gives one, its second gives two, and b has its own separate environment, so b's first call gives one. You'll see one, two, one. Two independent counters, from one function definition, each with private state that no other code can touch. That is a closure doing exactly what it should, and it's evidence our environments are right.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: Now string handling and logic. `let name = "Ember"; print("Hello, " + name + "!");` prints Hello, Ember!. And try `print(nil or "fallback");`, which gives fallback, and `print(1 < 2 and 2 < 3);` which gives true. If you try `print("a" + 1);`, you get our runtime error that operands of plus must be two numbers or two strings. And try calling a function before it's declared. Put `print(early());` at the very top and `fn early() { return "hoisted"; }` at the bottom. It works, thanks to the two-pass block. And switch the order of a `let`, you get an undefined variable error. Each of these is a language rule you implemented.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: Let me suggest some debugging tools that I use. First, add a flag to dump the tokens: if `process.argv[3] === '--tokens'`, print the token array and exit. Another for `--ast`, printing `JSON.stringify(program, null, 2)`. When something misbehaves, you can look at exactly which stage produced the wrong thing. If the tokens are wrong, the bug is in tokenizer.js. If the tokens are right but the tree is wrong, parser.js. If the tree is right and the output is wrong, interpreter.js. The staged pipeline gives you a clean place to put the blame, and the whole architecture pays off right here.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: Also, a REPL is easy now. Node's `readline` module gives you lines of input. For each line, we tokenize, parse and run it, against the same Interpreter instance, so definitions persist between lines. A tiny tweak: if the line is a bare expression without a semicolon, add one before parsing. Then you can type `1 + 2` and see the result. A REPL is just the pipeline in a loop. We won't write it out fully, but it's a good exercise, and it makes experimenting with the language a lot more fun than editing files.

lecture_title: 9.1 - Running a Real Program in Ember
text: Pause and look back at what you have. Roughly four hundred lines of JavaScript across tokenizer.js, parser.js, environment.js, interpreter.js and ember.js. A grammar written in BNF. A language with variables, functions, closures, recursion, conditionals, loops and short-circuit logic. Nothing is hidden behind a library. If someone asks how a language works, you can open these files and show them. In the last lecture, we'll look at what's missing and where you can take Ember next, and what the big languages do at those same decision points.

Let's wrap up with what we built, what's missing, and where to go next. We started with a blank folder and the question of what a language really is. Along the way we learned that a language is a grammar plus semantics plus an implementation. We borrowed from human grammar the ideas of categories, nested phrases and ambiguity. We separated syntax from semantics. We surveyed machine code, bytecode, compilers, interpreters, transpilers, AOT and JIT. Then we built the tokenizer, the recursive-descent parser, and the tree-walking interpreter with environments and closures. That's a lot, and every piece connects to the real languages you use daily.

Here is what Ember is missing, and each of these is a good next project. First, data structures: Ember has no arrays or objects. Adding an array literal means a new rule in the grammar, a new Array node in the parser, an indexing operation, and a new value type in the interpreter. Second, string escapes and a better number syntax. Third, a `for` loop, which you can implement as syntax sugar, by having the parser rewrite it into a while loop inside a block. That's called desugaring, and many real languages use it, because it keeps the interpreter small.

Fourth, better errors. Right now the runtime errors have no line numbers. Pass the line from the token into each node, and include it in messages. Fifth, a standard library of native functions, such as `len`, `str` and `clock`, defined in the globals just like `print`. Sixth, break and continue. Seventh, classes, which can be built on top of closures and environments, and are a wonderful way to see how object orientation really works. Pick one, do it, and notice that each addition touches the same three places: grammar, parser, interpreter. That regularity is the whole architecture paying you back.

You can also go deeper in different directions. Build a transpiler: walk the same tree and emit JavaScript source text, then run it with `eval` or write it to a file. Build a bytecode compiler and a small stack-based virtual machine, so you experience the speed difference first hand. Add a static check pass that runs between the parser and the interpreter, catching things like using an undefined variable before the program runs. These are exactly the stages we talked about in chapter three, and now you know enough to build any of them.

And a few books and resources, in the spirit of the course. Robert Nystrom's Crafting Interpreters is the best long-form treatment of exactly this territory, with a tree-walking interpreter in Java and a bytecode virtual machine in C. The ECMAScript specification is worth skimming now, because you'll recognize its language: it describes semantics step by step, like an interpreter. Reading the source of a small interpreter, such as Lua, will show you how a real, tiny, fast language is arranged. You have the vocabulary now: tokens, grammar, AST, environment, closure. Use it.

Last thought. When we started, a programming language felt like something that is given to you. Now it's something you can make, shape, and change. When you next hit a strange error message in JavaScript, or wonder why Python is built the way it is, you can reason about what its tokenizer, parser and evaluator must be doing. That's the real result of this course, more than Ember itself. Thank you for building along. Go write something in Ember, break it, extend it, and make it yours. Okay? Until next time, keep building.
